title: Demonstrable adequacy of a specification against intent and the environment

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a repeatable way to establish whether a software specification adequately expresses recorded stakeholder intent and fits the environment in which the software will operate. It would produce a reviewable package separating desired outcomes, descriptions of the environment, explicit domain assumptions, and the behavior required of the machine. It would then either expose a concrete disagreement or support a precisely bounded adequacy claim. This addresses an upstream assurance problem: proving that software satisfies a formal specification does not, by itself, establish that the specification describes the right system.

Proposed scope: every adequacy claim would identify the recorded intent being considered, the observable behavior used for comparison, the assumptions being made, and the class of scenarios covered. A disagreement could be expressed as a scenario in which the specification permits an unwanted outcome, excludes an intended outcome, or depends on an assumption that stakeholders dispute. Where requirements deliberately allow several designs, the method would preserve those alternatives rather than force a unique specification. Any completeness claim would be relative to this declared scope.

The target extends requirements elicitation and specification validation by seeking mechanically checkable arguments about the adequacy of the formal target itself. It remains dependent on observation and stakeholder judgment: unrecorded intent must first be elicited, and assumptions about physical systems or human behavior require evidence outside a proof checker. The supplied evidence motivates this capability without establishing either that it has been achieved or that every existing approach fails to provide it.

significance.text: Formal assurance establishes stated properties within a formal model and its assumptions. A system can therefore satisfy its proof obligations while omitting behavior users expect or relying on an inaccurate description of its operating environment. Anthropic’s verification report explicitly distinguishes proof checking from determining whether a specification matches reality; seL4’s account similarly acknowledges that proved properties may omit user expectations. Adequacy checking would extend assurance to the selection and interpretation of the specification.

Conditional significance: if the proposed capability worked with meaningful coverage and independently validated assumptions, stakeholders could evaluate repeatable adequacy arguments and inspect concrete disagreements before committing to an implementation. Coupled with implementation verification, this could reduce the risk of proving conformance to an inadequate target within the declared scope. Explicit assumptions would also make acceptance decisions more reviewable: stakeholders could distinguish what has been established formally from what still depends on observations or operational commitments. The supplied material provides no measured estimate of the resulting reduction in failures.

Further downstream possibilities are conditional synthesis. Reviewable specifications could become stronger inputs to certified synthesis, verification, procurement, and acceptance testing; explicit disagreements could help stakeholders resolve competing interpretations before code is written. These benefits would depend on the adequacy method’s coverage and on subsequent implementation assurance. The capability would not itself write code, discover every unrecorded hazard, recover all tacit intent, or establish that physical and human assumptions will continue to hold after deployment.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is an integrated method that moves from recorded stakeholder intent and environment observations to an explicit requirements package, then produces a checkable adequacy argument or a meaningful counterexample. Anthropic’s October 2026 report documents the difficulty of obtaining comprehensive, unambiguous specifications as an obstacle to verification at scale. It also identifies the separate problem of whether formal models describe reality. These are connected barriers: a precise specification can still omit an important requirement, and a valid proof can still depend on an inaccurate assumption.

Engineering synthesis: the method would need to retain traceable connections between stakeholder statements, observations, formal requirements, and assumptions. It would have to expose ambiguous or incompatible statements for adjudication, distinguish intentional underspecification from accidental omission, and define which observable differences matter. Informal, contradictory, or tacit intent should be treated as conditions the method must handle or elicit, rather than as fully characterized phenomena established by the supplied evidence. Unrecorded intent cannot be included in a guarantee simply by formalizing the available record.

Further scientific and engineering barriers concern the strength and meaning of the adequacy argument. A useful procedure must check that its assumptions and requirements are consistent, since inconsistent premises can make entailment vacuous. It must distinguish legitimate design alternatives from real disagreements and present counterexamples that stakeholders can understand and adjudicate. It must also separate a completeness result inside a declared scenario model from evidence that the model covers the deployed world. These are proposed obligations for the capability; the supplied materials do not establish a general solution.

Environment validation remains an empirical obligation. Observations may support an assumption about a device, operating system, workflow, or user population, but a mechanically checked argument cannot independently establish that an omitted environmental behavior never occurs. The breakthrough would therefore need to make such obligations explicit and connect them to evidence, rather than silently treating them as guaranteed facts.

current_state.text: Anthropic’s report dated 22 October 2026 identifies comprehensive and unambiguous specifications as a significant obstacle to verification at larger scale, using text editors and browsers to illustrate the difficulty of defining full correctness. For its main OSS-Fuzz effort, the report describes bounded no-crash proofs for selected executable entry points under stated machine and operating-system assumptions, including properties expressed through assertions. It also describes other behavioral verification case studies, so its results should not be characterized as exclusively crash-freedom. These achievements demonstrate verification of selected formal targets; they do not establish that those targets capture all intended behavior or every relevant environmental condition.

The seL4 proofs account describes substantial formal assurance while explicitly recognizing that user expectations about kernel behavior may fall outside the properties proved. It also identifies testing verified code against expectations as a way to test the specification. This preserves an important distinction: implementation proofs and specification validation address different questions, and the former does not eliminate the latter. The supplied review supports this reading from the proofs page; no additional conclusions are drawn here from the separately indexed manual, whose extraction was truncated and included pages without extractable text.

Leslie Lamport’s abridgement of the Amazon article published in Communications of the ACM in April 2015 distinguishes checking a design against desired properties from knowing that executable code implements the verified design. The account documents a gap in the practice reported at that time. It does not establish a universal limitation of TLA+, an inability to connect implementations to designs, or the state of all current industrial verification. The retained source is an abridged account of the original article, and its plain-text extraction does not preserve every visual distinction between original and editorial wording; the conclusion is therefore paraphrased at that limited scope.

The research notes identify Zave and Jackson’s 1997 article, Four dark corners of requirements engineering, as conceptual background for distinguishing requirements, environment descriptions, and machine specifications. They also identify Brun and colleagues’ 2026 Automatically Engineering Trusted Software: A Research Roadmap as discussing elicitation and formalization of user intent alongside synthesis and proof. Neither source has retained text in the supplied evidence. Their exact formulations, attributed conclusions, quotations, and detailed bibliographic particulars therefore remain unverified here. The proposed separation of requirements and assumptions can be retained as part of this innovation without treating those unavailable attributions as established evidence.

The supplied record supports a contemporary specification obstacle and several concrete distinctions between formal assurance and intended real-world behavior. It does not establish that the proposed integrated adequacy capability has been demonstrated. Equally, the empty bounded search record does not establish exhaustive openness as of 1 November 2026: absence of a retained demonstration is not proof that no relevant method exists.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: select a bounded domain such as a safety controller, payment ledger, or clinical workflow. Give two independent teams the same stakeholder record and environment observations. Each team produces a package that separates requirements, environment assumptions, and the machine specification, with traceability to the shared input. Before evaluation, declare the scenario class, observable vocabulary, adequacy relation, consistency checks, and permitted underspecification. These are proposed evaluation choices, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Two independent teams produce traceable separated packages from shared inputs

completion_criteria.text: A mechanical comparison should establish agreement on required observable behavior within the declared scope or return a distinguishing scenario for stakeholder adjudication. The evaluation should explicitly record legitimate design alternatives and unresolved disagreements. It should not require textually identical specifications or a single implementation where the requirements permit several. Consistency must be checked so that agreement is not obtained through contradictory premises, and agreement between teams must not be treated as sufficient evidence of adequacy because both teams can reproduce the same omission.
completion_criteria.label: Mechanical agreement on required observable behavior or a distinguishing scenario

completion_criteria.text: A complementary proposed test is a pre-registered corpus of historical requirement failures from the selected domain. Independent adjudicators should determine which failures were knowable from the recorded context, without relying on later information unavailable to the method. Evaluation should report which of those failures the method surfaces, which it misses, and which reported disagreements stakeholders reject. Success would demonstrate effectiveness across the tested cases; it would not prove completeness beyond the declared formal scope or literal universality across future environments.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-registered knowable failures surfaced, missed, and stakeholder-rejected disagreements

completion_criteria.text: For reproducibility, independent evaluators should be able to rerun the mechanical checks and reconstruct how each adequacy claim depends on the recorded inputs and assumptions. The package should identify empirical validation obligations, unresolved stakeholder decisions, and conditions that would invalidate its conclusions. Practical evaluation should report the human effort, computational resources, and stakeholder adjudication required, without inventing a universal acceptance threshold. A convincing result would combine reproducible formal arguments with independently assessed environmental evidence and clearly stated boundaries.
completion_criteria.label: Adequacy claims rerun and reconstructed with boundaries and resource costs

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: SWE-02, Certified synthesis of system-scale programs from reviewable specifications, is the closest downstream counterpart. SWE-03 asks whether a specification adequately expresses recorded intent and environmental constraints; SWE-02’s title concerns producing certified programs from reviewable specifications. A successful SWE-03 method could strengthen the input to such synthesis, while certified synthesis would still need its own implementation guarantees. Only SWE-02’s title was supplied, so a more specific dependency cannot be established.

Roster-based synthesis: SWE-01, Push-button verifying compilation for practical systems, and SWE-11, Proved semantics-preserving transformation of practical systems, concern assurance across implementation or transformation steps. SWE-03 concerns whether the behavior chosen as the target is adequate in the first place. Preserving or proving conformance to behavior and validating that behavior against intent are complementary obligations; success at either does not automatically discharge the other.

Roster-based synthesis: SWE-04, A compositional calculus for concurrent systems that fail, and SWE-10, Proof-carrying behavioral composition across trust boundaries, concern reasoning about interacting components. Their overlap with SWE-03 lies in making behavioral assumptions and obligations explicit. SWE-03 would additionally ask whether the selected component contracts and failure assumptions capture the relevant stakeholder needs and environment. SWE-08, Sequential meaning for fault-tolerant distributed execution, and SWE-09, Observable determinism as the default for parallel systems code, suggest particular behavioral targets whose adequacy could be examined; neither property is automatically the right requirement for every application.

Roster-based synthesis: SWE-05, Assurance that stays proportional to each behavioral change, concerns maintaining assurance as behavior evolves. SWE-03 could identify the requirements and environmental assumptions on which an adequacy argument depends, helping determine what must be reconsidered after a change. The distinction is between establishing the appropriateness of the target and maintaining assurance efficiently as the system or its context changes.

Roster-based synthesis: SWE-06, Sound behavioral recovery of legacy systems, concerns recovering existing behavior, which could inform an environment description or expose a discrepancy with stakeholder expectations. Existing behavior alone does not establish intended behavior. SWE-07, Practical confinement of general untrusted programs, concerns an enforceable behavioral boundary; SWE-03 would ask whether that boundary and its assumptions adequately express the protection stakeholders require. These relationships are inferred from the supplied titles and do not merge the innovations or establish their implementation details.

change_log.change: Preserved SWE-03’s identity while defining adequacy relative to recorded intent, explicit assumptions, observable behavior, and a declared scenario class.
change_log.reason: The review supports a substantial research target but does not establish universal access to intent, universal completeness, or the absence of all adequate existing methods.

change_log.change: Replaced the claim about how readily verification certifies the wrong system with a conditional reduction in the risk of proving conformance to an inadequate target.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence documents assurance gaps but provides no comparative measurement of failure reduction.

change_log.change: Integrated the distinction between formal proof, specification validation, and empirical validation of environment assumptions throughout the relevant sections.
change_log.reason: This is the central scientific distinction supported by the Anthropic and seL4 material and explains both the innovation’s value and its limits.

change_log.change: Refined the proposed independent-team demonstration to compare required observable behavior, with explicit consistency checks, permitted underspecification, and stakeholder adjudication.
change_log.reason: Identical specifications are unnecessarily restrictive, valid designs can differ, inconsistent premises can yield vacuous entailment, and teams can share omissions.

change_log.change: Expanded the historical-failure evaluation with independent judgments of knowability, reporting of misses and rejected disagreements, reproducibility, and practical evaluation boundaries.
change_log.reason: These refinements make the proposal more discriminating while preserving its status as a proposed demonstration rather than an established standard.

change_log.change: Corrected the description of Anthropic’s 22 October 2026 report to distinguish its main bounded no-crash effort from its other behavioral verification case studies.
change_log.reason: Characterizing the entire report as crash-freedom alone would omit supported scope identified by the review.

change_log.change: Restricted the Amazon design-to-code caveat to the practice reported in April 2015 and preserved the abridgement and extraction limitations.
change_log.reason: The evidence does not establish a universal or present-day limitation, and the retained text does not preserve every original-versus-editorial attribution.

change_log.change: Retained Zave–Jackson and Brun et al. as qualified research context while removing reliance on their unverified quotations and detailed formulations.
change_log.reason: No retained source text was supplied for either work; that limitation does not invalidate the independently supported concept.

unresolved_issues: The exact formulations and attributed conclusions of the Zave–Jackson article and Brun et al. roadmap remain unverified because their source text was not retained.
The supplied record does not establish whether an existing method already achieves some or all of the proposed integrated capability; exhaustive openness as of 1 November 2026 remains unestablished.
The adequacy relation, scenario language, treatment of underspecification, and strength of any scoped completeness claim still require concrete definitions for a selected domain.
The evaluation must determine how to adjudicate stakeholder disagreements and distinguish failures knowable from the original record from failures identifiable only in hindsight.
A practical method for detecting shared omissions and obtaining independent evidence for physical and human assumptions remains to be demonstrated.
Detailed relationships with SWE-02 and the other roster concepts remain limited by the availability of titles rather than full concept descriptions.

brief.title: Checking that software rules match people's needs
possible: Before commissioning software, people could check whether its specification—the written rules for what it must do—matches their recorded needs and its working environment. The check would either support that match within stated limits or produce a concrete scenario where the rules allow something unwanted or prevent something intended.
why: Software can follow its rules perfectly while leaving out something users need. Checking those rules against people's intentions could help developers and customers catch disagreements before building the system.

People approving software could see which conclusions follow from mathematical proof and which depend on assumptions about devices, workflows or users. That would make acceptance decisions easier to review.

sources.showed: The team proved that supported versions of seL4, an operating system's core, follow their specification. It also describes testing whether that specification meets developers' expectations.
sources.quote: seL4 has machine-checked mathematical proofs for the Arm, RISC-V, and Intel architectures.
sources.cited_for: Proofs that code follows its specification can leave user expectations outside their scope.
sources.not_established: A repeatable check that the specification captures recorded needs and environmental conditions remains to be demonstrated.

sources.showed: They used Claude to prove that selected ways of running open-source software avoid crashes under stated input limits and operating assumptions. They also explored proofs of other software behavior.
sources.quote: Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries.
sources.cited_for: Large-scale software proofs still depend on choosing appropriate rules and accurate models of the operating environment.
sources.not_established: Whether the proved rules capture all intended behavior and relevant environmental conditions remains unresolved.

sources.showed: This research roadmap discusses drawing out and formalizing user intent alongside software generation and proof.
sources.cited_for: It provides background on connecting user intent with mathematically checked software.
sources.not_established: A roadmap leaves the integrated method's effectiveness to be demonstrated.

sources.showed: This conceptual work examines distinctions between requirements, descriptions of the environment and machine specifications.
sources.cited_for: It provides background for keeping desired outcomes, environmental assumptions and software behavior distinct.
sources.not_established: These distinctions leave a working method for checking the specification against intent to be demonstrated.

sources.who: Chris Newcombe and colleagues at Amazon Web Services
sources.showed: Amazon engineers used automated checks of mathematical software designs to find subtle bugs. Their account also described an unresolved connection between checked designs and executable code.
sources.quote:
The model checker later found two bugs in other algorithms,
both serious and subtle.
sources.cited_for: Checking a design against desired properties can catch errors before implementation.
sources.not_established: The reported work leaves open whether the desired properties themselves adequately express stakeholder intent.

shown: The seL4 team has proved that supported software follows its specification. Anthropic and Theorem have proved selected software properties across many libraries. Amazon engineers have caught subtle design errors with automated mathematical checks.

These achievements establish behavior against chosen rules. A demonstrated, repeatable method for checking those rules against recorded human intent and observations of the environment remains the target.
missing: An integrated method must link recorded needs and observations to software rules, then produce a checkable argument or a concrete disagreement.
The checks must detect contradictory assumptions and preserve deliberately permitted design choices.
Reported disagreements must make sense to stakeholders, while shared omissions across teams must be exposed.
Assumptions about devices and people must connect to independent observations and explicit conditions for revisiting conclusions.

milestones.label: Independent teams trace their rules to shared inputs
milestones.explanation: Two teams would have to separate needs, environmental assumptions and software rules from shared inputs, with traceable links and agreed evaluation boundaries. This would test whether the process is repeatable.

milestones.label: Automated checks establish agreement or expose a disagreement
milestones.explanation: Checks would have to establish consistent agreement on required observable behavior or return a scenario for stakeholder judgment, preserving allowed choices. This would make disagreements concrete.

milestones.label: Historical failures, misses and rejected warnings are counted
milestones.explanation: A test set fixed in advance would need independent judgments of knowable failures, then counts of detections, misses and stakeholder-rejected warnings. This would measure usefulness without relying on hindsight.

milestones.label: Independent evaluators reproduce claims and measure their costs
milestones.explanation: Independent evaluators would have to rerun checks and reconstruct each claim's inputs, assumptions, limits, outstanding decisions and resource costs. This would test reproducibility and practical use.

uncertain: The meaning of an adequate match, the scenarios covered and the treatment of deliberately open design choices still need precise definitions.
How should evaluators resolve stakeholder disagreements and distinguish originally knowable failures from hindsight?
How reliably can a method detect shared omissions and obtain independent support for assumptions about people and physical systems?

page.title: Validation of formal software specifications
page.definition: A repeatable method establishes whether a formal specification—a mathematical description of required software behavior—captures recorded stakeholder intent under evidenced environmental assumptions. It produces a mechanically checkable adequacy argument or a concrete disagreement within declared observable behaviors and scenarios.

goal.need: Two independent review teams missed the A-7 aircraft requirements errors tabulated below; automated consistency checking found them in minutes. A study posted on 11 February 2021 covered two industrial examples and reported about 40 issues in a train-control requirements document. These results motivate validating requirements themselves alongside proving implementation conformance.

figures.caption: Automated consistency-checking findings reported in November 1998
figures.note: Both counts concern one revised A-7 aircraft requirements document.

statements.body: NASA, Office of the Chief Engineer
statements.quote: The project manager shall perform requirements validation to ensure that the software will perform as intended in the customer environment.
The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.

completion.title: An independent team reproduces a bounded adequacy argument for a formal software specification.
completion.criterion: For one bounded software application, a published method links recorded stakeholder intent and environmental evidence to separate requirements R, domain assumptions K and machine specification S. A proof checker accepts both S ∧ K ⇒ R and the consistency of S ∧ K. Stakeholders validate R, its interpretation and the design choices permitted by S; evidence independent of those proofs supports K. A separate team reconstructs these links and reproduces the checks from the recorded inputs. The claim covers only the declared observable behaviors and scenarios.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional test restricted to one bounded application.
completion.basis: Searches of NASA requirements-validation guidance, the accessible ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 preview, Zave–Jackson completion rules, the Brun roadmap and validation-obligation studies found no published acceptance test for an independently reproduced method combining mechanical adequacy checks with stakeholder and environmental validation. This test combines their constituent checks within one bounded application.

milestones.title: An abstract counterexample exposes a confirmed violation in the original requirements specification.
milestones.criterion: An abstract counterexample is executed against the original requirements specification and confirmed to violate a stated requirement. This excludes discrepancies introduced solely by abstraction. In November 1998, NRL reported this result for one contractor specification of a weapons-control panel: Spin found a safety-property violation and SCR simulation confirmed the corresponding behavior.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Naval Research Laboratory, SCR research programme, 1998 SCR/Spin study. The published demonstration concerns a weapons-control-panel specification.
milestones.threshold_quote: Simulation demonstrated that the safety violation was not spurious but an actual defect in the original specification.

milestones.title: A specification admits an implementation that meets its guarantees for every allowed environmental input.
milestones.criterion: For a reactive system, an implementation strategy exists that satisfies the specified guarantees for every input sequence satisfying the environmental assumptions. This is stronger than finding one jointly satisfying execution. In 2022, FRET researchers reported that 11 corrected requirements for one lift-plus-cruise concept aircraft were shown realizable in about 8 seconds.
milestones.set_by: Reactive-synthesis community; realizability definition stated by NASA Ames in Compositional Realizability Checking within FRET. The criterion concerns reactive systems, which continually respond to environmental inputs.
milestones.threshold_quote: for any sequence of inputs that satisfy the assumptions on the environment, the guarantees always hold.

milestones.title: A machine specification and domain assumptions imply the requirements without contradiction.
milestones.criterion: For requirements R, domain knowledge K and machine specification S, prove S ∧ K ⇒ R and prove S ∧ K consistent. S uses shared phenomena, does not constrain the environment and does not refer to the future. Evidence for implication includes one Arrival Manager example in a preprint posted on 11 August 2023: Event-B proof obligations establish modeled aircraft spacing of at least 3 minutes. A separate preprint, revised on 7 October 2026 and not peer reviewed, reports 12 clean/defective package pairs whose K proofs all pass, illustrating why proof success alone does not establish adequacy.
milestones.set_by: Requirements-engineering community, Zave and Jackson's completion rules, Section 6.3, criteria 3–5; author manuscript dated 16 July 1996.
milestones.threshold_quote:
This proof ensures that an implementation of S will satisfy the requirements.
(5) There is a proof that S and K are consistent.

milestones.title: Stakeholders validate the requirements, and reviewers check their traceability and environmental assumptions.
milestones.criterion: Reviewers check bidirectional traceability to stakeholder expectations and valid assumptions. All relevant stakeholder groups identify and remove defects; requirements are feasible, verifiable, unique and necessary. Evidence includes domain-expert use of visualizations to correct ETCS train-control requirements in the 2021 validation-obligation study. That study does not establish empirical validation of every environmental assumption.
milestones.set_by: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, Section 4.2.1.2.4, steps 2–6. These are requirements-review criteria; they do not prescribe a mechanically checked adequacy argument.
milestones.threshold_quote: Do the Requirements Satisfy Stakeholders? All relevant stakeholder groups identify and remove defects.

not_found: No independent reproduction establishing the combined completion criterion was located.
The full normative text of ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 was not accessible; its public preview was available.
The ACM-hosted roadmap and Zave–Jackson documents returned access errors; author-hosted copies were available.

results.finding: One seL4 kernel has functional-correctness proofs across verified configurations on 3 architectures.
results.detail: The page reports that verified C code behaves as specified, but does not establish an implementation strategy satisfying guarantees for every permitted environmental input sequence.
results.quote:
the C code of all verified
      configurations of seL4 behaves precisely as specified in the seL4
      specification and nothing more.

results.finding: For one seL4 kernel, the specification is proved to enforce 3 security properties in supported configurations.
results.detail: The page reports security theorems and assumptions, but does not establish the required R, K and S formulation or consistency of S ∧ K.
results.quote:
the specification, and
      by extension the kernel code, prevents an application running on top of seL4
      from modifying data without authorisation (integrity), from interfering
      with resource access of other applications (availability), and from
      learning information from other applications without explicit authorisation
      (confidentiality).

results.finding: No-crash proofs covered 239 entry points across 123 open-source libraries.
results.detail: The proofs concern compiled programs under modeled RISC-V and Linux semantics. The source does not establish a separate machine specification S, domain assumptions K and requirements R, or prove S ∧ K consistent.
results.quote: Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries.

results.finding: One DynamoDB fault-tolerance algorithm had a model-checked bug with a 35-step shortest error trace.
results.detail: The source reports a design bug but does not say the counterexample was executed against the original requirements specification or confirmed to violate a stated requirement.

results.finding: One contractor weapons-control panel specification: 1 safety-property violation confirmed by simulation.
results.detail: Spin found the violation in an abstracted specification; the SCR simulator reproduced the scenario in the complete specification, confirming an actual defect.
results.quote: Analyzing the reduced specification with the model checker Spin uncovered a possible safety violation. Simulation demonstrated that the safety violation was not spurious but an actual defect in the original specification.

results.finding: Liquid mixer: either of two 11-requirement specifications was realizable after removing one conflicting requirement.
results.detail: The original specification had 12 requirements and no environmental assumptions. Removing either LM-001 or LM-009 made the remaining specification realizable.
results.quote:
the rest of the specification is realizable when either[LM-001] or [LM-009]
are not part of it.

results.finding: One lift-plus-cruise aircraft specification was realizable with hover reached within 13 ticks.
results.detail: The result assumes wind speed stays within 20 knots and airspeed is nonnegative. Hover control mode was treated as a system-controlled output.
results.quote:
Strengthening the assumption to|wind_speed| <= 20
fixed the issue, as the requirements were shown to be realizable within 13 ticks, which makes
sense as kias needs to be reduced to zero for kgs to be<= 20, for any valid wind speed.

results.finding: Arrival Manager: 1 case study; Event-B proof addresses aircraft spacing of at least 3 minutes.
results.detail: The example provides evidence for a modeled spacing requirement, but the text does not establish S ∧ K consistency or all stated restrictions on S.
results.quote: After discharging the proof, we establish that our requirement is truly represented in the specification.

results.finding: In one ETCS case study, validation-obligation-inspired development uncovered around 40 requirements-document issues.
results.detail: Domain experts used visualizations to understand and correct issues. The study does not establish bidirectional traceability, validation by all relevant stakeholder groups, or empirical validation of environmental assumptions.

results.finding: For one liquid-mixer specification, five of six connected requirement components were realizable.
results.detail: Realizability bears on consistency, but the report does not prove that a separate machine specification and domain assumptions imply the requirements. The complete liquid-mixer contract was unrealizable.

results.detail: Realizability bears on consistency, but the report does not establish separate machine specification S and domain assumptions K, or prove S ∧ K ⇒ R and S ∧ K consistent.

fixed the issue, as the requirements were shown to be realizable within 13 ticks, which makes
